prompt:
Reddit post, r/houseplants.
Title: Croton has wilting leaves after repotting

I have repotted my Croton 10 days ago after noticing, that the soil it was in wasn’t really absorbing any water and bottom leaves drying out and dropping every week or so.

It was doing fine, but I noticed yesterday, that leaves started to wilt and I am unsure what to do.

The soil I used this time is 1:1:1 potting soil (fertilized), leca and pine barks.

What I noticed is, that the soil is quite wet (s. Last photo, watering indicator is fully blue) even though I watered last when I repotted the plant (10 days ago).

No, it was in the soil i bought it in before, which clearly wasn’t taking in any water and the plant was losing a bottom leave every 1-2 weeks.

I have humidifiers at home, humidity is about 50% usually

An automatic image classifier was also run on each photo. It only knows 5 classes:
- healthy: no visible problem
- watering: wilting or withering from too little or too much water
- fungal_bacterial: leaf spots, rust, anthracnose, blight, rot, bacterial wilt
- pest: visible insects or mites (trained almost only on cochineal scale on cactus)
- other: anything else, e.g. sunburn, nutrient or mineral problems, viruses, leaf tip necrosis, cold damage

The classifier is not perfect. It was trained mostly on curated dataset photos, not on phone photos like these,
and on such photos it is often wrong while still reporting a very high probability. Treat it as one weak hint:
rely on what you see in the photos and on the post first.

Classifier output (probability of each class):
Photo 1: healthy 76%, watering 23%, fungal_bacterial 0%, other 0%, pest 0%
Photo 2: watering 84%, healthy 16%, fungal_bacterial 0%, other 0%, pest 0%
Photo 3: watering 98%, healthy 2%, fungal_bacterial 0%, other 0%, pest 0%

What is wrong with my plant?
answer:
**Most likely cause: waterlogged roots from overwatering, probably made worse by poor drainage.**

The soil is still wet 10 days after repotting, and the moisture indicator reads fully wet. Wet soil with wilting leaves usually means the roots can't take up water, either because they're sitting in water or because they're damaged and rotting. Your old soil was draining poorly, so the roots may have been stressed before the repot, and the new mix may be holding water in the potting-soil portion. The decorative lace basket may also be trapping water if the terracotta pot doesn't drain freely into it.

**Less likely:**
- **Transplant shock.** Some wilting and leaf drop after repotting is normal, but a plant in dry-ish soil would usually perk up, and yours is sitting wet. If the soil dries out in a few days and the leaves still droop, shock is more likely.
- **Early root rot.** This is a serious version of the overwatering cause. Pull the plant out and check the roots. Firm, pale roots mean you're mostly dealing with saturation. Brown, mushy roots, or a sour smell, mean rot has started.

**Quick checks:**
1. Tip the plant out of its pot and look at the roots and drainage hole. Make sure the pot actually drains.
2. Push a finger or chopstick 5 cm into the soil. Wet or muddy means don't water yet.
3. Don't rely on the indicator stick alone in a bark and LECA mix. It may read the wrong way or be unreliable.

**Fix:**
- **Stop watering** until the top 3–5 cm is dry and the mix feels barely damp at depth. This may take a week or more.
- **Remove the plant from the decorative basket**, or make sure the inner pot drains freely. Standing water in the basket is a common cause of root problems.
- **If roots are brown or mushy**, trim them with clean scissors and repot into fresh, faster-draining mix in a pot with a drainage hole. Stiff, bark-heavy mixes drain better than potting soil alone.
- **Keep it in bright, indirect light away from drafts**, and leave the humidity as it is. Dropping leaves can still happen for a few weeks while the plant recovers.
